subtopic_detail: responding to knee pain with a restricted hip in an overweight adolescent whose knee imaging is normal
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy brought in by his father because of left knee pain that has been building over about six weeks and is now making him limp at school. He plays no organised sport and cannot recall an injury.

He weighs 71 kg with a body mass index above the 97th centile for age. He points to the front of his knee when asked where it hurts. The knee itself has a full range of movement without effusion, warmth or joint line tenderness, and the collateral and cruciate ligaments are stable. When you roll the left hip, he guards, and passive flexion of that hip produces obligatory external rotation. Radiographs of the knee taken in the department are reported as normal. He is afebrile, has had no rash or weight loss, and his inflammatory markers are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Left knee with full painless range and no effusion; left hip guarded on log roll with obligatory external rotation on passive flexion; antalgic gait
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein and white cell count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Radiographs of the left knee reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a bone scan of the pelvis and lower limbs to identify an occult stress injury
options.rationale: Scintigraphy is non specific, delivers a radiation dose, and would take days to arrange for a diagnosis that two plain films can make immediately. A stress injury is also improbable in a boy who does no organised sport. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee to look for an occult meniscal injury
options.rationale: Escalating knee imaging pursues a joint that examines normally and ignores the hip findings, and it is the single most common reason this diagnosis is missed for weeks. Referred pain travels along the obturator nerve from hip to distal thigh and knee, so the site of the pain is a poor guide to the site of the problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Make him non weight bearing and obtain urgent pelvic radiographs with frog lateral views
options.rationale: Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with knee pain points to the proximal femoral physis, and the frog lateral view is required because early displacement is often invisible on the anteroposterior film alone. Making him non weight bearing immediately matters because continued walking can convert a stable slip into an unstable one, which carries a far higher risk of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Prescribe ibuprofen with a graded quadriceps strengthening programme and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent is commonly patellofemoral and does respond to a loading programme, but that diagnosis requires a normal hip examination which he does not have. Six weeks of continued weight bearing is exactly the interval over which a stable slip progresses. (Source: RACGP: The Limping Child)

options.text: Aspirate the left hip under ultrasound guidance and send fluid for urgent microscopy and culture
options.rationale: Aspiration answers the question of septic arthritis, but he is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers and a six week history, which is the wrong tempo for infection. The near pair distinction is duration and fever: septic arthritis presents over days with systemic upset, not over six weeks in a well child. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Slippage of the proximal femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and peaks around the growth spurt, with obesity the dominant risk factor because it increases shear across a physis that is already widening under hormonal influence. Roughly a quarter of affected adolescents present with pain felt only in the thigh or knee, and every one of those is at risk of a delayed diagnosis if the hip is not examined. The most reproducible bedside sign is obligatory external rotation of the hip as it is passively flexed, which reflects the posterior and inferior displacement of the epiphysis. Radiographs must include a frog lateral view of both hips, since up to a fifth are bilateral and early slips can look normal on the anteroposterior projection alone. Treatment is surgical fixation in situ, and the single most important determinant of outcome is whether the slip was stable at the time of presentation.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee or thigh pain, whatever the knee examination shows.
Obligatory external rotation on passive hip flexion is the most useful bedside sign.
Request anteroposterior and frog lateral views of both hips, as up to 20 per cent are bilateral.
Make the patient non weight bearing at the moment of suspicion, before imaging confirms it.
An unstable slip, meaning one the child cannot weight bear on, carries a far higher risk of avascular necrosis.
explanation.pearls: A slip presenting before age 10 or in a child of normal weight should prompt screening for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, panhypopituitarism or renal osteodystrophy, since an endocrine cause underlies a substantial proportion of these atypical cases.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

subtopic_detail: recognising that a child presenting with vomiting and lethargy has a cardiac rather than gastrointestinal cause before giving fluid
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a busy emergency department on a Sunday evening. A 6-year-old boy has been referred by his general practitioner with three days of vomiting and lethargy after a household illness with fever and aches, and the triage note reads gastroenteritis for rehydration.

His mother says he has not had any diarrhoea at all, that he complains his tummy hurts under the ribs on the right, and that he has become breathless walking from the car. He has taken small amounts of fluid and has had three wet nappies overnight, which his mother thinks is normal for him. On examination he is mottled with cool peripheries and his liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. His chest has fine crackles at both bases. The nurse has drawn up a 20 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent and is waiting for your instruction.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 168, blood pressure 84/58, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 94 per cent in air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mottled with cool peripheries and capillary refill 4 seconds, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, fine bibasal crackles, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 3.4 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2), sodium 133 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 68 micromol/L (30 to 60)
data_table.Hydration: Three wet nappies overnight, no diarrhoea at any point

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Start oral rehydration solution by nasogastric tube at 25 mL/kg over the next four hours
options.rationale: Nasogastric rehydration is first line for mild to moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis that has failed oral intake, and it assumes the circulating problem is a fluid deficit. He has no diarrhoea, a normal urine output and an enlarged liver, all of which argue against a deficit. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Give intravenous ondansetron and observe for two hours before deciding on further treatment
options.rationale: An antiemetic treats the symptom that got him triaged and would let a child in cardiogenic shock sit unmonitored for two hours. Vomiting in this context is a manifestation of hepatic congestion and low cardiac output, not of gastric irritation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Give intravenous ceftriaxone after blood cultures and start a fluid resuscitation to 60 mL/kg
options.rationale: Escalating fluid to 60 mL/kg with antibiotics is the correct pathway for septic shock, and the fever and lactate make sepsis a genuine competing diagnosis worth covering. The finding that separates them is the combination of hepatomegaly and crackles, which belongs to a congested circulation rather than a vasodilated one. (Source: RCH CPG: Paediatric Sepsis)

options.text: Hold the fluid bolus and obtain an electrocardiogram, troponin and chest radiograph now
options.rationale: Hepatomegaly with bibasal crackles and shock in a child who has vomited without diarrhoea points to a failing myocardium rather than volume depletion, and a large bolus into a poorly contractile ventricle precipitates pulmonary oedema. The electrocardiogram, troponin and chest film are the three tests that establish the mechanism within minutes and redirect management towards inotropic support. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

options.text: Give the 20 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent and reassess the perfusion afterwards
options.rationale: A rapid 20 mL/kg bolus is correct in septic or hypovolaemic shock but is dangerous when the liver is already enlarged and the lung bases are already wet, because those two findings mark a ventricle that cannot accept the preload. This is the anti-pattern the presentation is built around, since the triage label makes the bolus feel automatic. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

explanation.summary: Myocarditis in childhood most often follows a viral illness and presents with non specific symptoms, so it is regularly mistaken for gastroenteritis, asthma or sepsis in the first hours of care. The features that should raise it are vomiting without diarrhoea, breathlessness out of proportion to the chest examination, right upper quadrant pain from hepatic congestion, and a heart rate that stays high after fever and distress are addressed. Hepatomegaly with crackles in a shocked child is the bedside pairing that separates cardiogenic from distributive or hypovolaemic shock. Fluid in cardiogenic shock is given, if at all, in small aliquots of 5 to 10 mL/kg with reassessment after each, and the mainstay is early inotropic support and paediatric intensive care involvement. Presentation can progress to arrhythmia or cardiac arrest within hours, which is why the electrocardiogram cannot wait.
key_points: Vomiting without diarrhoea is a red flag against a gastroenteritis label in a shocked child.
Hepatomegaly plus crackles points to cardiogenic rather than septic or hypovolaemic shock.
Persistent tachycardia that does not settle with antipyretics and analgesia warrants an electrocardiogram.
Give fluid in 5 to 10 mL/kg aliquots with reassessment after each when the heart is the problem.
Troponin, brain natriuretic peptide and echocardiography confirm the diagnosis and guide intensive care referral.
explanation.pearls: Low voltage QRS complexes across all limb leads, with T wave inversion and any ventricular ectopy, is the electrocardiographic signature that should stop a fluid bolus in a child labelled as gastroenteritis.

subtopic_detail: interpreting jaundice persisting beyond two weeks in a breastfed infant whose nappies show pale stools
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general practice liaison clinic. A 3-week-old girl is brought in because she is still yellow. She was born at term by normal delivery, went home on day 2, and is exclusively breastfed.

Her mother says she feeds hungrily every three hours, has gained weight steadily, and is otherwise content. When you ask about the nappies, her mother says the poo has gone a pale creamy colour over the past week and that the wee stains the nappy darker than it used to. The maternal and infant blood groups are both O positive and the direct antiglobulin test taken on day 2 was negative. The newborn screening card was normal, including the thyroid result. Her weight today is 3.85 kg, up from a birth weight of 3.42 kg.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced to the thighs, alert and vigorous, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, no bruising or petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 168 micromol/L with a conjugated fraction of 74 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), gamma glutamyl transferase 412 U/L (less than 100)
data_table.Growth and history: Weight 3.85 kg from a birth weight of 3.42 kg, exclusively breastfed, newborn screening card normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start phototherapy and recheck the total serum bilirubin after twelve hours of treatment
options.rationale: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin into water soluble isomers and does nothing for a conjugated fraction that is already water soluble, and in cholestasis it can produce the bronze baby discolouration. The near pair distinction is which fraction is raised, which is exactly why the split bilirubin must be requested rather than the total alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Advise a 48 hour trial of formula feeding and repeat the bilirubin once the trial is complete
options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding to demonstrate a fall in bilirubin is an outdated test for breast milk jaundice, undermines lactation, and again addresses the unconjugated fraction only. It would waste two more days in an infant whose surgical window is measured in weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Repeat the direct antiglobulin test and send a reticulocyte count and blood film for haemolysis
options.rationale: A haemolytic workup investigates an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and the identical maternal and infant blood groups with a negative direct antiglobulin test on day 2 have already argued against it. Haemolysis also does not produce pale stools, because the bile pigment that colours stool is still being made. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is a benign pattern and review the bilirubin again in two weeks
options.rationale: Reassurance fits an unconjugated prolonged jaundice in a thriving breastfed infant, and the good weight gain and contented baby make that label tempting, but the conjugated fraction and the pale stools take this out of that category entirely. Two weeks of waiting at 3 weeks of age consumes a large part of the window in which surgery still works. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric liver service for investigation of a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
options.rationale: A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total, or above roughly 25 micromol/L, is never physiological and combined with pale stools and dark urine it demands urgent specialist investigation for biliary obstruction. Referral is urgent rather than routine because the outcome of surgery for biliary atresia falls sharply once the infant passes about 60 days of age. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term infant, or beyond 21 days in a preterm infant, requires a split bilirubin in every case, because the common benign cause and the one time critical surgical cause are clinically indistinguishable at the cot side. Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated, occurs in a thriving baby, and resolves over weeks to months without intervention. Biliary atresia produces a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with pale acholic stools and dark urine, and the infants characteristically look well and gain weight early on, which is precisely what disarms the clinician. Outcomes after the Kasai portoenterostomy depend heavily on age at surgery, with the best results before 45 to 60 days and a steep decline thereafter. Every infant with a conjugated fraction needs same week specialist assessment rather than a watchful review.
key_points: Any jaundice persisting past 14 days in a term infant requires a split, not a total, bilirubin.
A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total or above about 25 micromol/L is always pathological.
Pale stools with dark urine indicate obstructed bile flow and are the key history question to ask.
Thriving and contentedness do not exclude biliary atresia in the first two months of life.
Kasai portoenterostomy performed before 45 to 60 days gives substantially better long term outcomes.
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to compare the nappy against a printed stool colour card rather than describing the colour in words, since pale acholic stool is commonly reported as yellow and the visual comparison is what converts a vague history into a referral.

subtopic_detail: arranging surveillance for asymptomatic eye disease in a young child with a persistently swollen knee and a positive antinuclear antibody
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old girl whose left knee has been swollen for four months. Her parents noticed she was stiff and reluctant to walk for the first half hour each morning but that she plays normally by mid morning.

She has never had a fever, rash or weight loss, and there is no history of trauma or preceding illness. Her knee is swollen with a small effusion and lacks the last 10 degrees of extension, and no other joint is involved. Her eyes look entirely normal to you and to her parents, she has no eye pain, no redness and no photophobia, and she has not complained about her vision. Her inflammatory markers are within normal limits, her rheumatoid factor is negative, and her antinuclear antibody is positive at a titre of 1 in 320.

data_table.Examination: Left knee warm with a small effusion and a 10 degree fixed flexion deformity, all other joints normal, eyes white and quiet
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate within normal limits, rheumatoid factor negative, antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 320
data_table.History: Four months of morning stiffness lasting about 30 minutes, no fever, rash or weight loss

lead_in: In addition to treating the joint, what surveillance would you arrange?

options.text: Slit lamp examination by an ophthalmologist every three months regardless of eye symptoms
options.rationale: A young child with few involved joints and a positive antinuclear antibody sits in the highest risk group for chronic anterior uveitis, which is asymptomatic and produces a white quiet eye until irreversible damage has occurred. Only slit lamp examination detects the anterior chamber cells at a stage where topical treatment prevents cataract, band keratopathy and glaucoma. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.text: Visual acuity testing by the practice nurse every three months with referral if acuity falls
options.rationale: Acuity stays normal until the uveitis has already caused structural damage, and a 3-year-old cannot reliably perform the test in any case. The near pair distinction is that acuity measures the consequence whereas the slit lamp detects the process. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.text: Ophthalmology review arranged only if she develops eye pain, redness or light sensitivity
options.rationale: Symptom triggered review is the default reasoning for most eye disease and is precisely what fails here, because the chronic anterior uveitis of childhood is painless and the eye stays white. Waiting for symptoms means the first presentation is often a cataract or a distorted pupil. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

options.text: Annual fundoscopy through a dilated pupil performed in the general paediatric outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Fundoscopy examines the posterior segment while this disease lives in the anterior chamber, and an annual interval is far too long for a condition that can cause damage within months. The correct instrument and the correct interval are both wrong in this option. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.text: Repeat antinuclear antibody titres every three months and refer if the titre continues to rise
options.rationale: The antibody is used once, to stratify risk and set the screening interval, and serial titres do not track uveitis activity or predict its onset. Following the titre instead of the eye substitutes a blood test for the examination that actually detects disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the commonest form in Australian children, typically affecting a young girl with one or a few large joints and normal inflammatory markers, which is why a normal C reactive protein never excludes it. The associated chronic anterior uveitis is the complication that determines long term disability, and it is entirely silent in its early stages. Risk is highest in children under seven at onset, with few joints involved, and with a positive antinuclear antibody, and screening intervals are set accordingly, most often three monthly in this highest risk group and extending as the child ages and the disease settles. Treatment of the joint itself usually begins with intra-articular corticosteroid, with methotrexate added for persistent or polyarticular disease. Screening continues for years after the arthritis is quiescent, because uveitis can appear or recur long after the joint has settled.
key_points: Normal inflammatory markers are common in oligoarticular disease and do not argue against the diagnosis.
Chronic anterior uveitis in this group is painless and the eye remains white until damage is established.
Highest risk is young age at onset, few joints, and a positive antinuclear antibody.
Slit lamp examination is the only adequate screening test, since the disease is in the anterior chamber.
A persistent fixed flexion deformity and limb length discrepancy are the joint level consequences of undertreatment.
explanation.pearls: Untreated anterior uveitis produces posterior synechiae that tether the iris to the lens, so an irregular or sluggishly reacting pupil found on routine examination in a child with arthritis means the disease has been active for months and needs same day ophthalmology assessment.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

subtopic_detail: distinguishing a fused suture from a positional head shape in an infant with progressive skull asymmetry
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 5-month-old boy referred because of an odd head shape that his parents say is getting worse rather than better, despite four months of alternating his sleeping position and daily supervised tummy time as advised by the child health nurse.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and has no torticollis on examination, with full and symmetrical neck rotation to both sides. Looking down on his head from above, the skull is long from front to back and narrow from side to side, and the ears sit symmetrically. You can feel a firm raised ridge running along the midline from the anterior fontanelle backwards, and the anterior fontanelle itself feels small for his age. His head circumference is tracking along the 50th centile and his development is age appropriate, with good head control and early rolling.

data_table.Examination: Skull elongated anteroposteriorly and narrowed biparietally, palpable firm midline ridge, small anterior fontanelle, ears symmetrically positioned, full neck rotation bilaterally
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile and tracking, weight and length on the 50th centile
data_table.Development: Good head control, rolling front to back, social smile and babbling present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue repositioning and tummy time with review of the head shape in a further three months
options.rationale: Repositioning is the correct treatment for a deformational head shape, and four months of it with worsening rather than improvement is the history that argues against that diagnosis. Persisting with it here delays surgery past the age at which the simplest operations are possible. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Refer to a craniofacial service and arrange skull imaging to assess the sutures
options.rationale: A ridged suture with a head that is long and narrow, symmetrical ears and a shape that has worsened despite repositioning indicates a fused sagittal suture rather than a positional moulding, and this requires surgical assessment. Referral is time sensitive because endoscopic strip craniectomy with helmeting is generally restricted to infants under about six months, after which open vault remodelling becomes necessary. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for management of neck tightness contributing to the head asymmetry
options.rationale: Physiotherapy is central where torticollis drives a positional flattening, but his neck rotation is full and symmetrical in both directions, which removes the mechanism. The near pair distinction is that positional flattening produces an asymmetrical parallelogram shape with one ear pushed forward, whereas his skull is symmetrically narrowed. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Arrange a moulding helmet through an orthotist and review the response after eight weeks
options.rationale: Helmet therapy redirects growth through open sutures and cannot reshape a skull whose suture has already fused, so it would waste the remaining months of rapid brain growth. Helmets have a defined role after endoscopic surgery but not as an alternative to it. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Measure thyroid function and vitamin D and review once metabolic causes have been excluded
options.rationale: Metabolic bone disease can distort the growing skull, but rickets softens bone and produces frontal bossing and craniotabes rather than a ridged fused suture. His growth and development are normal, which further argues against a systemic metabolic cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

explanation.summary: Most abnormal head shapes seen in infancy are deformational and follow sustained supine positioning, which is a tolerable trade against the large reduction in sudden infant death that back sleeping achieved. Deformational plagiocephaly produces an asymmetrical parallelogram when viewed from above, with the ipsilateral ear and forehead displaced forward, and it improves with repositioning, tummy time, and treatment of any coexisting torticollis. True suture fusion produces a characteristic symmetrical distortion determined by which suture is involved, with sagittal fusion giving a long narrow skull, and it worsens rather than improves as the brain grows. A palpable ridge, a shape that deteriorates despite conservative measures, or a head circumference crossing centiles all warrant craniofacial referral. The functional risks of untreated multi-suture disease include raised intracranial pressure and visual loss, while single suture disease is more often an issue of head shape and skull growth.
key_points: Viewed from above, positional plagiocephaly is a parallelogram whereas sagittal fusion is long and narrow.
A positional head shape improves with repositioning; a fused suture worsens as the brain grows.
A palpable ridge along a suture line with a small anterior fontanelle points to fusion.
Check neck rotation in every infant with an abnormal head shape, since torticollis drives positional flattening.
Endoscopic strip craniectomy with post-operative helmeting is generally limited to infants under about six months.
explanation.pearls: Sagittal synostosis is the commonest single suture fusion and the head circumference stays on its centile, because the skull compensates by growing front to back, so a normal head circumference offers no reassurance against it.

subtopic_detail: choosing between a surgical and an endocrine cause of vomiting in a second week infant when the electrolytes contradict the expected pattern
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department at 11 pm to see a 12-day-old boy who has been vomiting after feeds for four days. His mother says the vomits shoot out and that he seems hungry straight afterwards, and the referring letter from the after hours general practitioner reads query pyloric stenosis, for surgical review.

He was born at term at 3.40 kg after an uncomplicated pregnancy and weighs 3.05 kg tonight. He is lethargic, mottled and poorly perfused with a capillary refill of 4 seconds, and he does not rouse fully for the examination. His nappy is dry. There is no palpable abdominal mass after a test feed and no visible peristalsis. His genitalia appear normal for a male infant with both testes descended, and the newborn screening card result is not yet available. The venous gas and electrolytes have just returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 186, blood pressure 52/28, respiratory rate 58, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Lethargic and mottled with capillary refill 4 seconds, dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanelle, soft abdomen with no palpable mass, normal male genitalia with both testes descended
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 119 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), chloride 96 mmol/L (98 to 108), glucose 2.1 mmol/L (2.6 to 5.5), pH 7.19 with bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22 to 28)
data_table.Weight: 3.05 kg tonight against a birth weight of 3.40 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give hypertonic sodium chloride 3 per cent 4 mL/kg to correct the sodium before other treatment
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for hyponatraemic seizures or obtundation attributable to cerebral oedema, and here the low sodium is a marker of aldosterone deficiency with salt wasting rather than a free water excess. Correcting the number without replacing the missing hormone leaves the underlying loss running. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis)

options.text: Give sodium chloride 0.9 per cent 20 mL/kg with intravenous fludrocortisone and dextrose 10 per cent
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is the long term mineralocorticoid and has no parenteral form, and it is the wrong drug for an acute crisis in any case. Hydrocortisone is chosen precisely because at stress doses it delivers both glucocorticoid and sufficient mineralocorticoid effect, which is the near pair distinction being tested. (Source: APEG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

options.text: Give sodium chloride 0.9 per cent 20 mL/kg with intravenous hydrocortisone and treat the potassium
options.rationale: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and a metabolic acidosis in a collapsed second week infant is the biochemical signature of mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency, and hydrocortisone must be given at the same time as volume resuscitation rather than after it. Delaying steroid until a cortisol result returns is the error that turns a treatable crisis into an arrest, so the sample is drawn and the drug given without waiting. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis)

options.text: Give sodium chloride 0.9 per cent 20 mL/kg and refer to the surgical team for pyloromyotomy
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from losing gastric acid, which is the exact inverse of his acidotic, hyperkalaemic, low chloride picture, and no mass was palpable after a test feed. The projectile vomiting and hungry rebound are genuine shared features, which is why the electrolytes rather than the history decide this. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Give sodium chloride 0.9 per cent 20 mL/kg with intravenous cefotaxime after blood cultures
options.rationale: Late onset sepsis is a legitimate competing diagnosis in a collapsed neonate and antibiotics are commonly given alongside, but sepsis does not by itself explain the combination of a sodium of 119 mmol/L with a potassium of 7.4 mmol/L. Treating only the infection would leave the steroid deficiency uncorrected and the infant would not improve. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Salt wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically presents in the second week of life, once the protective effect of maternal and placental steroid has worn off, and boys are at particular risk because they have no ambiguous genitalia at birth to trigger earlier investigation. The presentation overlaps almost completely with the far commoner pyloric stenosis in its history, since both produce forceful non bilious vomiting in a hungry infant of the same age, and the separation is biochemical. Loss of aldosterone drives urinary sodium loss with potassium and hydrogen retention, producing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and a metabolic acidosis, while cortisol deficiency adds hypoglycaemia and impaired vascular tone. Treatment is simultaneous volume expansion, glucose, and stress dose hydrocortisone, with the diagnostic samples for cortisol and 17 hydroxyprogesterone drawn before the first dose but never allowed to delay it. Newborn screening for this condition is not performed uniformly across all Australian jurisdictions, so a normal or pending card cannot be relied on to exclude it.
key_points: Pyloric stenosis gives a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis; adrenal crisis gives hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemic acidosis.
Male infants with salt wasting disease have normal genitalia and so are not detected at birth on examination.
Draw cortisol and 17 hydroxyprogesterone before the first hydrocortisone dose, but never delay the dose for the result.
Hydrocortisone at stress doses provides enough mineralocorticoid activity for the acute phase.
Hyperkalaemia in this setting warrants an electrocardiogram and treatment in its own right alongside volume expansion.
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone for an infant in adrenal crisis is given as 25 mg intravenously as the initial bolus, followed by 25 mg over the next 24 hours as a divided or continuous dose, with the same 25 mg figure used for children under three years.
